title: Tenali Raman and the Blindfolded Philanthropist

full_text:
A wealthy merchant of Vijayanagara named Dhanpal boasted throughout the city of his boundless religious charity. To prove that his philanthropy was 'pure, selfless, and untainted by favoritism', he announced an extraordinary ritual:
Every Friday morning, he sat on a raised platform outside the main city gates, tied a thick black silk blindfold over his eyes, and distributed silver coins from a large copper bowl to anyone who touched his hands.
He boasted: 'My charity is truly blind! I give without looking, asking no questions of caste, merit, or need!'

Tenali Raman observed that this theatrical spectacle was being shamelessly exploited:
A gang of robust, lazy gamblers and healthy tricksters stood in line repeatedly, changing their voices, receiving dozens of coins each, while truly blind orphans, crippled elders, and sick widows were pushed into the gutters by the aggressive mob.

Tenali resolved to cure Dhanpal of his vain, foolish ritual.

The following Friday, Tenali arrived at the distribution platform carrying an enormous basket filled with coarse river pebbles and jagged pottery shards.
As Dhanpal reached into his bowl to hand out silver coins blindly, Tenali stepped onto the platform, took Dhanpal’s hand, placed a large, jagged, sharp granite stone into the merchant’s palm, and closed his fingers over it!

Dhanpal yelped in pain:
'Ouch! What is this? Who has placed a sharp, jagged stone in my hand?'
He ripped off his black silk blindfold, glaring in furious anger:
'Who dared do this to a noble benefactor?'

Tenali stood before him, smiling calmly:
'Why, noble Dhanpal! Why did you remove your blindfold?
You proudly boast that your charity is blind, and that you give without looking.
If your charity is blind, why should your hands complain when they receive stones instead of gold?
Look around you!'

Tenali pointed to the crowd:
'Look at these twenty strong, able-bodied young gamblers laughing behind the trees with bags of your silver, while yonder crippled grandmother and blind orphan weep in the ditch with empty hands!
Heaven gave you eyes not to blindfold them for public applause, but to seek out genuine suffering and wipe away real tears.
Blind charity is not virtue; it is lazy vanity that feeds parasites and starves the truly needy!'

Dhanpal looked at the sharp stone in his hand, then looked at the suffering poor in the gutters.
His heart filled with profound remorse.
He threw away his blindfold, apologized to Tenali, and restructured his philanthropy, visiting the homes of the disabled, funding orphanages, and ensuring that his charity was guided by open eyes, discernment, and genuine love.
moral: Charity done for theatrical vanity without discernment feeds frauds while true need goes unassisted.
